items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: shoot one time I worked with Charlie Parker. He was one of the people that influenced me to come to New York.

ctx.x: I remember you saying when you first heard bop that you were with a group of people who, obviously somebody had introduced it to you who said this is great stuff, and the other people or person you were with said no, no, no, don’t play that.

Yeah the man I was playing with: “You don’t want to play that garbage.” And the first time, I was very young then, I was maybe 17 or 18, somewhere in there, and I heard a young alto player who was playing like Charlie Parker, and I had never heard Charlie Parker before I heard this alto player. He was about my age. And wow, it just touched me, and he had his buddy, who was playing trumpet like Dizzy. In fact in Chicago they used to call this guy “Little Diz.” And it turned me on. So I started playing like Bud ©…

Powell, because I started listening to records, and I was working with this group which was primarily a rhythm and blues group, that’s what you would call it today. And strange enough, the saxophone player and the drummer in the group were also turned on by bebop. So the drummer just got tired of brow beating. You know, “Man why don’t you play straight, what are you dropping all those bombs for?” And he quit. And after a while the saxophone player quit. And I quit too because he replaced them with people who…

items.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995…
items.q: I went over to his house and he had these old Dial 78s. And he played them for me, and I said wow, I hadn’t heard anything like that.

ctx.x: I mean did you feel like you had too much, I don’t know how to put this, too much knowledge from your bebop playing?

That could be it. I felt like I was playing too much because you know, like when you get in the habit of playing like the modern changes, or as you say, bebop, it doesn’t fit with © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

what they’re doing. You’ve got to think one-three-five, you know what I’m saying? You don’t deviate from that one-three-five or one-four. And you stay in that bag all the time. You can’t play those slick changes like Charlie Parker was playing you know.
